title: 1 Chronicles 5:11–22
context: The Chronicler moves to Gad, settled beside Reuben in Bashan and Gilead. The Gadite leaders named here differ from the sons of Gad listed in Genesis 46:16 and Numbers 26:15–17, and the Chronicler gives his own record without harmonizing. These lists are dated to the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel (5:17), the latter usually taken to be the second king of that name. The passage then gathers Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh into one account of war with the Hagrites and with Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab (5:18–22). Jetur and Naphish appear among the sons of Ishmael in Genesis 25:15, and some readers connect these peoples with them, but the identifications of all four groups are uncertain. The Chronicler stresses that the eastern tribes cried to God in the battle and he answered them because they trusted in him, and that the war was of God. Arminian and Reformed readers share this ground: God hears those who call on him and gives victory as he wills, and the note that they lived there until the captivity (5:22) prepares for the account of their unfaithfulness and exile.

verses.text: The sons of Gad lived beside them in the land of Bashan to Salecah:
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the sons of Gad lived beside Reuben in the land of Bashan as far as Salecah, consistent with the eastern allotment described in Joshua 13. The verse places the tribe in its inheritance and continues the Chronicler’s survey of the people God settled on both sides of the Jordan.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the verse as part of the record of God’s distribution of the land, including the territories east of the Jordan. Both traditions agree that the precise boundaries are not the point, and that the Chronicler wishes his readers to remember the eastern tribes as fully part of Israel’s inheritance.

verses.text: Joel the chief, Shapham the second, Janai, and Shaphat in Bashan.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that Joel the chief, Shapham the second, Janai, and Shaphat are named as Gad’s leaders in Bashan. These names differ from the sons of Gad in Genesis 46:16 and Numbers 26:15–17, and the Chronicler records his list without explaining the difference, perhaps reflecting a later period of the tribe’s history.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the difference from the earlier lists and do not attempt to harmonize it, since the text offers no explanation. Both traditions agree that the verse honors the leaders of Gad as part of the remembered order of the tribe, and that God’s preservation of Gad is the thread running through the list.

verses.text: Their brothers of their fathers’ houses: Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, Zia, and Eber, seven.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that seven brothers of their fathers’ houses are listed, including Michael and Meshullam. The count of seven summarizes the group, and the verse shows how the Chronicler organized families within a tribe, reflecting a people whose households were known and whose belonging to Israel was remembered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the orderly listing as a reflection of the Chronicler’s concern for structure within God’s people. Both traditions agree that the names have no recorded deeds here, yet their inclusion testifies that God kept the families of Gad within his covenant people across generations.

verses.text: These were the sons of Abihail, the son of Huri, the son of Jaroah, the son of Gilead, the son of Michael, the son of Jeshishai, the son of Jahdo, the son of Buz;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that Abihail’s line is traced back through many generations to Buz, including a Gilead and a Michael. The long chain of descent roots these Gadite families in a remembered past, which mattered greatly for a community seeking to recover its identity after the disruption of exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the careful tracing of descent and see it as an expression of God’s faithfulness through the generations. Both traditions agree that the names should not be identified with similar names elsewhere without evidence, and that the verse serves the Chronicler’s purpose of showing continuity within Israel.

verses.text: Ahi the son of Abdiel, the son of Guni, chief of their fathers’ houses.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Ahi son of Abdiel, son of Guni, is named as chief of their fathers’ houses. The verse identifies leadership within the clan, and the Chronicler’s attention to such heads shows a people organized under recognized leaders who bore responsibility for their families.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the naming of a chief as part of the order God sustained among the tribes. Both traditions agree that the verse adds little narrative but contributes to the picture of Gad as a structured people with known leadership, preserved within the covenant community.

verses.text: They lived in Gilead in Bashan and in its towns, and in all the pasture lands of Sharon as far as their borders.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that Gad lived in Gilead, in Bashan and its towns, and in the pasture lands of Sharon to their borders. Many interpreters take this Sharon to be a pasture region east of the Jordan rather than the better-known coastal plain, though the location is uncertain. The verse emphasizes land suited to flocks.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise leave the identification of Sharon open and see the verse as a description of the inheritance God gave Gad. Both traditions agree that the pasture lands reflect the pastoral way of life of the eastern tribes, recalling their request for land suited to livestock in Numbers 32.

verses.text: All these were listed by genealogies in the days of Jotham king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam king of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the genealogies were recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel, usually taken to be Jeroboam the son of Joash. The dating anchors the lists in a specific period shortly before the Assyrian deportations that the chapter will describe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly observe the chronological marker and note that the text does not say whether the two reigns overlapped or whether the reference covers a broader period of record-keeping. Both traditions agree that the Chronicler is pointing to a time of record-keeping before the exile, which gives the coming account of captivity added weight.

verses.text: The sons of Reuben, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, of valiant men, men able to bear buckler and sword, able to shoot with bow, and skillful in war, were forty-four thousand seven hundred sixty that were able to go out to war.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh together had forty-four thousand seven hundred sixty valiant men skilled in war. The verse emphasizes their strength and preparation, which makes the following statement that they cried to God in the battle all the more striking.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the size and skill of the army and see the verse as setting up the contrast between human strength and divine help. Both traditions agree that the Chronicler does not despise military preparation but will insist that victory came because the tribes trusted God rather than their own numbers.

verses.text: They made war with the Hagrites, with Jetur, and Naphish, and Nodab.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the eastern tribes made war with the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab. Jetur and Naphish appear among the sons of Ishmael in Genesis 25:15, and some readers connect these peoples with them, though the identification of all four groups is uncertain and the text does not explain the cause of the war.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly hedge the identifications and do not supply a reason for the conflict that the text does not give. Both traditions agree that the verse names the enemies in order to set the stage for the Chronicler’s main point in the next verse: the tribes’ dependence on God in battle.

verses.text: They were helped against them, and the Hagrites were delivered into their hand, and all who were with them; for they cried to God in the battle, and he answered them because they put their trust in him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers stress that the tribes cried to God in the battle and he answered them because they put their trust in him. The verse presents a real relationship in which God responds to the faith of his people, and Arminian readers see here an encouragement that trusting God in a time of need is never in vain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm the same truth: God helped those who cried to him and answered them because they trusted in him. They see both the trust and the answer as gifts of God’s grace, while honoring the real prayer the tribes offered. Both traditions agree that the Chronicler presents this as a model of seeking God, a theme central to his whole history.

verses.text: They took away their livestock: of their camels fifty thousand, and of sheep two hundred fifty thousand, and of donkeys two thousand, and of men one hundred thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the large numbers of livestock and people taken: fifty thousand camels, two hundred fifty thousand sheep, two thousand donkeys, and one hundred thousand people. The numbers emphasize the scale of the victory, and readers recognize that such figures in Chronicles raise questions that interpreters approach in different ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the size of the spoil and the varied interpretive approaches to large numbers in Chronicles, without settling the question here. Both traditions agree that the point of the verse is the completeness of the victory God gave, and that the taking of people as captives belongs to the harsh realities of ancient warfare that the text reports.

verses.text: For many fell slain, because the war was of God. They lived in their place until the captivity.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the Chronicler’s explanation that many fell because the war was of God, and that the tribes lived in their place until the captivity. The verse affirms God’s involvement in the victory while quietly foreshadowing that the land so gained would later be lost through unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the phrase that the war was of God as an affirmation of God’s sovereign governance of the battle and its outcome. Both traditions agree that the closing reference to the captivity links this victory with the exile described in 5:25–26, showing that God’s gifts call for continued faithfulness.
